title: Health costs connect care choices, household adaptation, institutional response, and contested legitimacy
source_unit: US household, panel, institutional, and randomized evidence layers; units remain source-specific
geography: United States, with Oregon randomized evidence

denominator.unit: weighted SHED population estimate; source-specific valid fields

observations.method: Federal Reserve SHED 2025 care-skipping and household adaptation analysis with source-specific valid-field denominators.
observations.uncertainty: Cross-sectional self-report; no dated bill, causal order, treatment consequence, or political follow-up.
observations.subgroup: US adults/households represented by SHED 2025 estimates.
observations.counterinterpretation: Reported foregoing can reflect need, access, coverage, recall, or cost jointly.

observations.period: 2024 to 2025 SHED recontact panel; care-foregoing paths

denominator.unit: persistent-care-foregoing recontact respondents with complete care fields

observations.method: Link 2024 and 2025 SHED records by shedid; classify any Yes among listed care-foregoing fields and weight 2025 outcomes by panel_weight.
observations.uncertainty: Longitudinal descriptive transition; no dated bill, causal order, remedy, or replicate-weight standard errors.
observations.counterinterpretation: Persistence may reflect ongoing illness, access, coverage, prices, or repeated unrelated needs.

observations.period: 2008 lottery; Oregon Medicaid first-year and follow-up outcomes

denominator.unit: randomized lottery treatment-control contrasts; published estimates

observations.method: Random assignment by Oregon Medicaid lottery among low-income uninsured adults, linked to survey and credit outcomes.
observations.uncertainty: Historical local experiment; does not identify a particular bill, household alternative, current national effect, or trust outcome.
observations.counterinterpretation: Coverage can expand use and reduce measured financial exposure without changing every health or labor outcome.

denominator.unit: de-identified credit records in CFPB analysis

observations.method: CFPB analysis of de-identified credit records and regulatory response history.
observations.uncertainty: Credit outcome is not the complete household burden; policy effects vary by reporting rule and the 2025 rule was later vacated.
observations.subgroup: Consumers and census tracts represented in CFPB credit-reporting analysis.
observations.counterinterpretation: Collections may proxy underlying financial distress and cannot alone identify the original care decision.

observations.method: Two randomized medical-debt relief experiments with administrative credit, health, utilization, and financial-wellness outcomes.
observations.uncertainty: Relief and reporting conditions are study-specific; null average outcomes do not rule out heterogeneous or longer-term effects.
observations.subgroup: Participants in randomized medical-debt relief experiments.
observations.counterinterpretation: Credit repair can be real while health or care repair remains absent or unmeasured.

observations.period: July 2026 Census HTOPS; expense difficulty and institutional confidence

denominator.unit: weighted cross-source contrast with source-specific valid denominators

federal_statistics_confidence_contrast.unit: percentage points; expense difficulty minus no difficulty

congress_confidence_contrast.unit: percentage points; expense difficulty minus no difficulty

observations.method: Matched framing contrast across Census household financial-pressure and institutional-confidence measures; not a same-person medical-bill causal estimate.
observations.uncertainty: Separate survey constructs and dates; no health-bill attribution, remedy timing, trust trajectory, or political-action measure.
observations.subgroup: HTOPS respondents grouped by reported difficulty paying usual household expenses.
observations.counterinterpretation: Expense difficulty and institutional confidence can share common causes or selection without one causing the other.

boundary: This record is a layered synthesis, not a same-unit causal chain. The decisive missing link is a dated health-cost episode followed through care choice, household adaptation, institutional remedy, and later trust or action.
